### 4

- **refined** (ch-004 chunk 3 (editor's notes: Timbuktu, Songhai, Mali)): The Hakluyt editor (Brown, 1896, drawing on Barth) says Timbuktu was founded by the Tuareg about 1087-8, that its great mosque and palace were built by Mansa Musa with Ishak es-Saheli as architect, but that Sankore is generally regarded as the oldest mosque; Leo's Askia material is second-hand from merchants and his dates are confused (Askia took power in 1493, pilgrimage 1495, Katsena expedition 1513, Agades 1515, Mali absorbed 1501); Gao was Askia's usual capital; Leo's 'Sonni Heli' is Sonni Ali, who took Timbuktu in 1468-9 and Jenne earlier; Ahmad Baba's chronicle is cited for Musa's pilgrimage. These are 19th-century editor's notes: usable only as pointers. They support the course's Timbuktu-architect wording and the caution that Sankore is a mosque cluster, but add a founding date (1087-8, Tuareg camp site) that is tradition [TRADITIONAL DATE]. Quote nothing.
- **extended** (ch-004 chunk 1 (Book VII: Tombuto, Gago, Melli, Guber, Agadez, Cano)): Leo (Pory 1600; Leo wrote about 1526 from visits in the 1510s): Tombuto town founded (he says) by a king Mense Suleiman in 610 AH, houses of chalk and thatch, a stone-and-lime temple and a palace built by a Granada architect, many cloth weavers, books from Barbary sold for more than any other goods, a camel-load of salt sold for 80 ducats, a rich king with gold plates, 3,000 horsemen and poisoned-arrow footmen, a king who hated Jews, cowries (400 to a ducat), half the town burned in five hours; Gago: unwalled, rich merchants, slave market (a fifteen-year-old for six ducats), horses fetching 40 to 50 ducats; Askia (Izchia) conquered Guber, Cano, Casena, Gualata and made Agadez tribute-paying. Leo is an outsider of the 1510s and later: read beside the Tarikh es-Sudan, and his account of Askia Muhammad's conquests is hearsay [PROBABLE]. Names are in 1600 English and OCR is poor. Quote nothing.
- **extended** (ch-004 chunk 2 (Hausa states, Guangara, Borno, Gaoga, Nubia)): Leo (about 1526) on the Hausa lands and Kanem-Borno: Cano, Casena, Zegzeg, Zanfara made tributary by Askia (Ischia); Guangara kept 7,000 archers and 500 horsemen, with gold lands to the south reached by slave porters; Borno's king had 3,000 horsemen and paid for horses in slaves, fifteen or twenty slaves for one horse, often making merchants wait up to a year; Gaoga (Chad-Nile) ruled by a former slave who bought horses; Nubia's Dangala had ten thousand families. Editor's notes (Brown, 1896) call Askia 'perhaps the greatest sovereign of Negroland' and say Leo's Askia information is second-hand from merchants who disliked him. Fits Module 4 lesson 4 (Hausa states, Kanem-Borno) and the horses-for-slaves point in Module 8. Reader gives ten to fifteen slaves a horse on the coast; Leo twenty at Borno [PROBABLE].

### 3

- **extended** (ch-003 chunk 1 (Book VI: Numidian villages, Dara, Segelmesse)): Leo, Book VI chunk 1: Numidian oasis towns trade with the land of Negros; the Dara province had goldsmiths and artisans on the Tombuto to Fez road, kept slaves from Negroland and exported indigo; Segelmesse (Sijilmasa) was a rich, walled town with colleges before its destruction, its merchants taking Barbary goods south for gold and slaves; Venetian ships carried goods to Mesrata for slaves, musk and civet from the south; tolls of a quarter ducat per camel load. Outsider view of the north end of the Sahara routes in the early 1500s; Module 3 lesson 3 is the use. Quote nothing.
